name: AI for Marketing and Community Outreach
objectives: Given one program and one audience, write a key message that says what it is, why it matters to them and what to do next, in one or two sentences

Given your key message, draft four social media posts with AI: an announcement, a behind-the-scenes post, a thank-you and a last-chance reminder, each short, ending with one action, and using only photos and stories with consent
Given your program notes, write a 200-word newsletter article with one story, one true number and how to help, with every number, name, date and quote checked
Given an outreach draft, rewrite it in plain language and draft a translation for your community, with the translation checked by a fluent speaker before sharing
Given your posts and flyer, write alt text and make them accessible with captions, contrast and readable hashtags, with alt text that matches what is really in each image
Given your outreach pieces and event date, create a four-week outreach calendar with week, channel, piece and who posts, with dates checked against your real calendar

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Knowing your audience and your message
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write one clear key message for one audience.
This lesson builds toward: Given one program and one audience, you will write a key message that says what it is, why it matters to them and what to do next, in one or two sentences.
Good outreach speaks to one group at a time. Volunteers, donors, families you serve, church members and local businesses each care about different things.
A key message says, in one or two sentences, what you want that audience to know and do. Example for parents: "Free after-school tutoring starts September 8 at the community center. Sign up by September 1 so your child has a seat."
AI can help you sharpen it. Ask: "Here is our program: [public details]. Write three versions of a one-sentence message for [audience]. Each should say what it is, why it matters to them, and what to do next."
Step by step:
- Choose one program and one audience.
- Write what you want them to know and do.
- Ask AI for three one-sentence versions.
- Pick the clearest one and edit it.
Words to know:
- Audience: the group of people you are trying to reach.
- Key message: the one or two sentences you most want your audience to remember and act on.
Try it now: Pick one program and one audience. Use AI to get three versions of a key message, then write your final one at the top of a page titled "Outreach plan".
You can now write a clear key message for one audience.

check.q: Why should outreach speak to one group at a time?
options: Different groups care about different things
Social media allows only one group
Donors and volunteers are the same people
check.why: Volunteers, donors, families and businesses each care about different things.

check.q: Your message to volunteers does not say what to do next. What do you add?
options: A longer history of the organization
One clear action, such as "Sign up by Friday"
check.why: A key message says what it is, why it matters and what to do next.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing social media posts with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft four social media posts for one program with AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given your key message, you will draft four social media posts with AI: an announcement, a behind-the-scenes post, a thank-you and a last-chance reminder, each short, ending with one action, and using only photos and stories with consent.
Social media posts work best when they are short, show a real moment, and end with one clear action. Different platforms suit different lengths: a Facebook post can be longer, an Instagram caption goes with a photo, and a post on a short-text platform must be brief.
Ask: "Using this key message: [message], write four social media posts for [platform] over four weeks: an announcement, a behind-the-scenes post, a volunteer or participant thank-you, and a last-chance reminder. Under 60 words each, friendly, with one call to action."
Use your own photos with permission. Never post photos of children or clients without written consent, and never share someone's story with details that could identify them unless they agreed.
Step by step:
- Give AI your key message and platform.
- Ask for four post types over four weeks.
- Edit each to sound like your organization.
- Pick photos you have permission to use.
Words to know:
- Platform: a social media service, like Facebook or Instagram.
- Caption: the text that goes with a photo or video post.
- Consent: a person's agreement, ideally written, to be shown or quoted.
Try it now: Use AI to draft four posts for one platform from your key message. Edit them and add them to your outreach plan.
You can now draft a series of social media posts with AI.

check.q: Which kind of post must be brief?
options: A post on a short-text platform
check.why: A post on a short-text platform must be brief; a Facebook post can be longer.

check.q: A participant shared a moving story but did not agree to be named. How do you post it?
options: Post their photo with the story
Share it only without identifying details, or not at all
check.why: Never share someone's story with identifying details unless they agreed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Drafting a newsletter article
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn program notes into a short newsletter article with AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given your program notes, you will write a 200-word newsletter article with one story, one true number and how to help, with every number, name, date and quote checked.
Newsletters keep donors, volunteers and members close. A short article tells one story: what happened, who it helped (no private details), what it means for the mission, and what readers can do next.
Give AI your notes: "Turn these notes into a 200-word newsletter article for our supporters. Use a friendly headline, one short story, one true number, and end with how to help: [notes]."
Check the number and every name and date. Add a quote only if a real person said it and agreed to be quoted. If you send email newsletters, include a clear way to unsubscribe and follow your email tool's rules.
Step by step:
- Write rough notes about one recent moment.
- Ask AI for a 200-word article with a headline, story, number and how to help.
- Check every fact and quote.
- Add it to your newsletter with a photo you may use.
Words to know:
- Newsletter: a regular update sent to supporters by email or on paper.
- Unsubscribe: a link that lets someone stop getting your emails.
Try it now: Write five lines of notes about a recent program moment. Use AI to turn them into a 200-word newsletter article. Check every fact.
You can now turn program notes into a checked newsletter article.

check.q: How many stories should a short newsletter article tell?
check.why: A short article tells one story.

check.q: AI's newsletter draft adds a quote from a volunteer who never said it. What do you do?
options: Remove it, or ask the volunteer for a real quote they agree to
check.why: Add a quote only if a real person said it and agreed to be quoted.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Plain language and other languages
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to rewrite outreach in plain language and draft a translation for review.
This lesson builds toward: Given an outreach draft, you will rewrite it in plain language and draft a translation for your community, with the translation checked by a fluent speaker before sharing.
Many people in your community read in a second language, read at a basic level, or are busy and skim. Plain language helps everyone: short sentences, common words, the most important thing first.
Ask: "Rewrite this at a 6th-grade reading level. Short sentences. Put the date, place and how to sign up first." Then: "Translate this into Spanish for families in our community."
AI translations can be wrong or sound strange. Always have a fluent speaker from your community check a translation before you share it.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to rewrite your text at a 6th-grade reading level.
- Put date, place and action first.
- Ask for a translation into a language your community uses.
- Have a fluent speaker check it.
Words to know:
- Plain language: writing people can understand the first time they read it.
- Reading level: how easy text is to read; a lower grade level is easier.
Try it now: Take your key message and one post. Ask AI to rewrite them in plain language and translate them into a language your community uses. Note who could check the translation.
You can now make outreach plain and draft translations for a fluent speaker to check.

check.q: Which is part of plain language?
check.why: Plain language uses short sentences, common words and the most important thing first.

check.q: AI translated your flyer into Vietnamese and no one on staff speaks it. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to check its own translation
Find a fluent speaker from your community to check it first
check.why: AI translations can be wrong, so a fluent community speaker checks them before sharing.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making outreach accessible
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write image descriptions and make posts and flyers easier for everyone to use.
This lesson builds toward: Given your posts and flyer, you will write alt text and make them accessible with captions, contrast and readable hashtags, with alt text that matches what is really in each image.
Accessible outreach works for people who are blind or have low vision, are deaf, or use a screen reader. Alt text is a short description of an image that a screen reader reads aloud.
AI can draft alt text: "Write alt text under 125 characters for a photo of volunteers sorting cans at a food drive." Check it describes what really is in the photo.
Other easy wins: put captions on videos, use strong color contrast on flyers, do not put important words only inside an image, and write hashtags with capital letters (#FeedOurCity) so screen readers say them correctly.
Step by step:
- Write alt text for every image (AI can draft it).
- Add captions to videos.
- Use strong contrast on flyers.
- Keep key details in the text, not only in the image.
- Capitalize each word in hashtags.
Words to know:
- Alt text: a short written description of an image, read aloud by screen readers.
- Screen reader: software that reads screen text aloud for people who are blind or have low vision.
- Contrast: how different the text color is from the background.
Try it now: Write alt text for the photos with your four posts, using AI to draft and you to check. Fix any hashtags so each word starts with a capital.
You can now make posts and flyers accessible with alt text, captions and clear design.

options: People who use a screen reader
check.why: A screen reader reads alt text aloud for people who are blind or have low vision.

check.q: Your flyer has the date and place only inside a picture. What do you change?
options: Put the important details in the text too
check.why: Screen readers cannot read words inside an image.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Planning a month of outreach
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put your outreach pieces on a four-week calendar.
This lesson builds toward: Given your outreach pieces and event date, you will create a four-week outreach calendar with week, channel, piece and who posts, with dates checked against your real calendar.
A simple calendar keeps outreach steady. List four weeks. For each week, write what goes out, on which channel, and who posts it.
AI can suggest a schedule: "Here are my pieces: [list]. Our event is on [date]. Make a four-week outreach calendar as a table: week, channel, piece, who posts." Check the dates against your real calendar.
Afterward, look at what worked: sign-ups, comments, shares, replies. Keep doing what brought people in.
Step by step:
- List your pieces: posts, newsletter, flyer.
- Ask AI for a four-week calendar table.
- Check dates against your real calendar.
- Assign who posts each piece.
- After the month, note what brought people in.
Words to know:
- Content calendar: a schedule of what you will post or send, and when.
- Channel: a way you reach people: social media, email, flyers, announcements.
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-month outreach plan. Put your key message, four posts with alt text, newsletter article and plain-language flyer text on a four-week calendar.
You can now plan and draft a month of nonprofit outreach with AI.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Audience and key message No single audience, or the message has no next step. One audience and a one- or two-sentence message with what, why and what to do next. Learner tried three versions and can say why they chose this one. Four social posts Fewer than four posts, or a photo or story without consent. Four short posts of the four types, each ending with one action, with consent for all photos and stories. Each post fits its platform's length. Newsletter article A number, name, date or quote is not checked. About 200 words, one story, one true number and how to help, all checked. Includes a real quote the person agreed to. Plain and accessible Flyer is hard to read, or images have no alt text. Plain-language flyer with key details first, and alt text for every image that matches the photo. Also has a translation checked by a fluent speaker and readable hashtags. Four-week calendar No calendar, or dates do not match the real calendar. A four-week table with week, channel, piece and who posts, dates checked. Notes how results will be tracked after the month. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What do you look at after a month of outreach?
options: Only how many posts you made
check.why: Look at what worked: sign-ups, comments, shares and replies.

check.q: AI's calendar puts the last-chance reminder after your event date. What do you do?
options: Move it to before the event, checking dates against your real calendar
check.why: Check AI's dates against your real calendar.
